claims.text: Thus Spoke Zarathustra is a four-part work of speeches and episodes by Friedrich Nietzsche, published between 1883 and 1885 and listed in the standard reference account among his mature works.

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
citations.quote: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883–5), Beyond Good and Evil (1886),

claims.text: It is not a treatise: its hero is a prophet-figure whom Nietzsche had in mind from youth and finally identified with a Persian, to give a view of history in which each era has its prophet.

citations.title: Introduction by Mrs Forster-Nietzsche
citations.quote: “but in the end,” he declares in a note on the subject, “I had to do a PERSIAN the honour of identifying him with this creature of my fancy.

citations.title: Introduction by Mrs Forster-Nietzsche
citations.quote: Persians were the first to take a broad and comprehensive view of history.

claims.text: Nietzsche's sister Elisabeth, who wrote the introduction in this edition, calls it his most personal work, the history of his experiences, friendships, ideals and disappointments.

citations.title: Introduction by Mrs Forster-Nietzsche
citations.quote: “Zarathustra” is my brother’s most personal work; it is the history of his most individual experiences, of his friendships, ideals, raptures, bitterest disappointments and sorrows.

items.heading: A Europe losing its Christian footing

claims.text: Nietzsche's famous claim that "God is dead" is not simply atheism: it says that Christianity no longer gives Europe a shared basis for ethics, and that morality built on it is bound to collapse.

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
citations.quote: Christianity no longer commands society-wide cultural allegiance as a framework grounding ethical commitments

claims.text: His sister's introduction sums up his target in the same terms: Christianity, as a product of the resentment of the weak, has undermined everything that promotes life.

citations.title: Introduction by Mrs Forster-Nietzsche
citations.quote: He assumes that Christianity, as a product of the resentment of the botched and the weak, has put in ban all that is beautiful, strong, proud, and powerful

items.heading: An older ideal of rearing great individuals

claims.text: The Superman was not invented for this book: his sister says the ideal appears in his writings of 1873-75, rooted in the youthful belief that the object of mankind should lie in its highest individuals.

citations.title: Introduction by Mrs Forster-Nietzsche
citations.quote: The notion of rearing the Superman is only a new form of an ideal Nietzsche already had in his youth

items.heading: A philosopher without a post, on the move

claims.text: Nietzsche became professor of classical philology at Basel in 1869 at age 24, but ill health forced him to resign the chair by 1879, which freed him to write.

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
citations.quote: culminating in May 1869 when he was called to a chair in classical philology at Basel.

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
citations.quote: by 1879, he was forced to resign his professorship altogether.

claims.text: Afterwards he settled into spending winters near the Mediterranean, usually in Italy, and summers in Sils Maria, Switzerland.

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
citations.quote: settling into a pattern of spending winters near the Mediterranean (usually in Italy) and summers in Sils Maria, Switzerland.

claims.text: The central idea, eternal recurrence, came to him on a walk at Sils Maria in August 1881.

citations.title: Ecce Homo: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
citations.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
citations.quote: The basic conception of the work, the idea of eternal recurrence, the highest formula of affirmation that can possibly be attained − belongs to the August of the year 1881

citations.title: The first summer: 1881
citations.quote: His first stay already prompted a key idea which turned his philosophy in a new direction: “the idea of eternal recurrence”

claims.text: Part I came to him in the winter of 1882-83 at Rapallo, on the Italian coast near Genoa, in poor health and in a small hotel by the sea.

citations.title: Ecce Homo: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
citations.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
citations.quote: it was during this winter and under these unfavourable conditions that my Zarathustra came into existence.

claims.text: He wrote Part II and drafted Part III at Sils Maria in the summer of 1883.

claims.text: The Wagners' friendship with Nietzsche effectively ended when he sent them Human, All-too-human in early 1878.

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

claims.text: Around the time of the book's start he had an intense but painful friendship with Paul Rée and Lou Salomé, a Russian student; after he unsuccessfully proposed marriage, Salomé and Rée left for Berlin.

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
citations.quote: At the beginning of this period, Nietzsche enjoyed an intense but ultimately painful friendship with Rée and Lou Salomé

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

claims.text: He says the closing section of the first part was finished at the hour of Richard Wagner's death in Venice, in February 1883.

citations.title: Ecce Homo: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
citations.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
citations.quote: was completed precisely at that sacred hour when Richard Wagner died in Venice

claims.text: Nietzsche was a frequent guest in the Wagner household from his early Basel years; the friendship lasted into the mid-1870s, and its break was a key touchstone in his life.

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

citations.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

claims.text: Nietzsche calls the period between The Gay Science and Zarathustra one pregnancy: the earlier book gives the opening of Zarathustra and its fundamental idea.

claims.text: The Superman is the ideal of a higher future humanity, not a person already existing; his sister says it cannot be understood apart from the Order of Rank, the Will to Power and the Transvaluation of all Values.

citations.title: Introduction by Mrs Forster-Nietzsche
citations.quote: In general the doctrine of the Superman can only be understood correctly in conjunction with other ideas of the author’s, such as:—the Order of Rank, the Will to Power, and the Transvaluation of all Values.

citations.title: Introduction by Mrs Forster-Nietzsche
citations.quote: Never yet hath there been a Superman.

claims.text: Nietzsche says the type of Zarathustra can only be grasped through what he calls great health.

citations.title: Ecce Homo: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
citations.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
citations.quote: To understand this type one has first to become clear as to its physiological presupposition: it is that which I call great health.
